issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in this profile. With assault trauma, the other trigger items (related sounds, being naked) plausibly cue danger/vulnerability, and the threat items are about danger and vigilance. Praise/positive attention points in a very different interpersonal direction and is not supported by corresponding appraisals or threat content, so it weakens cross-node coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
issues.explanation: 'Fear going crazy' is poorly aligned with the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize external danger and vigilance, and the trigger pattern centers on assault-related cues. A dominant appraisal of losing one's mind would usually be accompanied by threat content about internal loss of control or dissociation-like danger, which is absent here.

For an assault trauma, the trigger pattern strongly suggests a sexual assault context (being naked, being looked at sexually). That is not impossible, but the rest of the profile does not support that specific context strongly enough to make the set cohere: there are no matching sexual-assault-linked threat or memory items, and the only bodily appraisal is about the body being unreliable rather than violated or contaminated.

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'I can no longer trust my own body' is more typically linked to injury, dissociation, panic-like bodily cues, or medical trauma. It does not fit well with the mainly sexual-vulnerability trigger pattern unless there is additional supporting content, which is absent here.

vignette:
Mai was seventy-one when she finally agreed to speak in detail about what had happened, though the event itself still arrived in her mind with the force of something immediate. She had been living in the United States for decades, working as a lawyer, and had built a life that was orderly, demanding, and public. The assault occurred when she was alone and not expecting danger, and what stayed with her most was not only the violence itself but the humiliating way it was accompanied by the experience of being looked at sexually, as if she had been reduced to an object in someone else’s gaze. In the aftermath, she found that ordinary sounds could throw her back into the same tightened, alarmed state. A sudden noise behind her, a voice that sounded too close, or related sounds that resembled the sensory edges of the assault could make her shoulders jerk and her attention snap toward the source before she had fully registered what she was hearing. The reaction was bodily and instant, and she would feel her own heart pounding so hard that it seemed to fill her entire chest.

In the weeks that followed, Mai noticed that she no longer trusted her body in the way she once had. She had been the kind of person who relied on competence and composure, but now she was unsettled by the sudden surge of her own heartbeat, by the fear that her body could tip her into panic without warning, or that it might betray her in some other, less predictable way. She described this in practical terms, saying that when her heart raced she could not convince herself that she was safe, because the sensation itself felt like proof that something was wrong. At work, where she was still engaged with legal matters, she became acutely aware of time passing in meetings, on phone calls, and while waiting for documents or replies. If something took longer than expected, she immediately assumed something bad was happening. A delayed response from a client, a late arrival, or an unanswered call was enough to put her on edge, scanning through possibilities she knew were not always reasonable but could not dismiss. She had come to believe that she had to be on guard all the time, because danger could appear without warning and because waiting, for her, had become almost intolerable.

As the months went on, Mai also noticed how differently night felt from day. During daylight she could still move through her routines, but after dark she had much less sense of ease, and she found it harder to feel safe at night. The dimness of evening, the quiet of the house, and any unexpected sound in the dark seemed to enlarge her sense of vulnerability. She and her husband had shared their home for years, yet even there she remained watchful after sunset, listening longer than she used to before settling into bed, and being reluctant to relax fully once the house grew still. She had also become increasingly aware of the way other people’s looks affected her. If she sensed she was being looked at sexually, even briefly, she experienced an immediate tightening and discomfort that made her want to withdraw. What might once have been brushed off as a passing stare now felt loaded and exposing, as though being seen in that way carried the possibility of danger and humiliation.

Mai spoke about these experiences with a mixture of restraint and clear distress. She described having strong negative feelings that were hard to contain: fear, horror, anger, and shame all seemed to exist close together, and she did not experience them as fleeting. They could rise in ordinary moments, leaving her feeling suddenly flooded and unsettled, especially when one of her triggers appeared or when she was left alone with her thoughts. Over time, she had come to see the world as a dangerous place, and this conviction sat alongside her wish to continue functioning as she always had. As a lawyer, she had spent her life assessing risks and managing details, but now the everyday world felt less predictable and less trustworthy. She remained married and continued to carry herself with dignity, yet those close to her could see that she was more guarded, more alert to what might go wrong, and less able to dismiss the sense that she needed to watch everything around her.

What finally brought Mai to seek help was the accumulation of these moments: the pounding heart that startled her, the silences that made her imagine something bad was happening, the unease that settled over evenings, and the way reminders in public could make her feel exposed or unsafe. She did not want her life to keep narrowing around vigilance and fear. More than anything, she hoped to feel at home in her own body again, to move through day and night without constantly bracing for threat, and to reclaim some sense that the world could still contain ordinary safety.
